extracted.intended_audience: advertising and marketing professionals, creative teams, and brand strategists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating humorous video advertising that both wins creative awards and resonates with general audiences, using emotional-response testing (System1's Test Your Ad) and star-rating benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional use of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Over half the Film Lions winners (52%) were intentionally funny, up from 43% last year — showing a return to humor as an award-winning element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer purposeful, intentionally funny creative when appropriate; trend indicates humor is back in vogue. Example: Apple’s “RIP, Leo” and McDonalds’ “Raise Your Arches.” Anti-pattern: relying on accidental or ambiguous attempts at humor that audiences don't clearly register as funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke measurable emotional response
rubrics_metrics.description: System1's Test Your Ad platform measures viewers' emotional responses to predict commercial impact — 'the more people feel, the more they buy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ads to produce strong, measurable emotions (positive where possible) and validate via emotional-response testing. Use measured outcomes (e.g., Star Rating) to predict short- and long-term commercial potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unresolved or dominant negative emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Many award-winning ads mix humor with substantial negative emotions (sadness, fear, anger, disgust); when negative aspects influence overall response and crowd out positive emotion, ads become less effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If negative emotions are used (edgy or dark humor), resolve them early and clearly so they don't dominate audience reaction. Anti-patterns: pushing negative elements hard without resolution, relying on shock/negativity that alienates viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor must resonate beyond the marketing bubble
rubrics_metrics.description: Edgy humor that makes marketers laugh often fails to connect with the world outside the marketing bubble; juries and marketers can have different comedic tastes than the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test humor with broad, representative audiences rather than relying only on insider reactions. Aim for widely-shared understandability and emotional appeal, not just industry in-jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose types of humor that can have broad appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Fun ideas, surreal executions and edgy humor — including surreal, satirical and slapstick comedy — can have broad public appeal when done well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider surreal, satirical or slapstick executions as routes to both jury recognition and public appeal (examples: McDonalds’ surreal eyebrow meme, Marmite’s fake-documentary, Apple’s slapstick). Ensure execution is accessible and relatable so it translates outside industry circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand purpose can succeed but must deliver strong emotional storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose-driven ads were far less common among winners this year; the successful purpose ad (Apple’s 'The Greatest') succeeded through inspirational stories and an addictive soundtrack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pursuing purpose-driven creative (non-charity/NGO), prioritize powerful inspirational storytelling and production (music, pacing) to generate emotional engagement. Anti-pattern: purpose messaging without strong emotional craft will underperform relative to humor-led creative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume awards equal higher mass-market effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cannes winners on average hit 2.1 Stars on Test Your Ad compared to the global average of 2.2 Stars — awarded work still isn’t testing better than the average video ad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always validate award-winning or jury-favored creative against mass-market benchmarks; use testing rather than awards as proxy for commercial effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star Rating benchmarks and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: System1's Star Rating scale (out of a possible 5.9) is used to quantify ad performance; examples: McDonalds’ 'Raise Your Arches' scored 4.7 Stars; 3-Stars is an indicator of notable performance (Apple had two 3-Star ads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use star ratings as concrete targets: 3+ Stars indicate solid performance; 4+ Stars indicate strong public appeal. Compare ads to category/global averages and to awarded peers when assessing likely commercial impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use testing tools and filters to compare performance
rubrics_metrics.description: System1 suggests viewing US and UK winning ads on the Test Your Ad platform and filtering by country (Global) and category (Cannes Lions 2023) to see how winners performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the Test Your Ad platform (or equivalent tools) to filter and benchmark specific cohorts (e.g., Cannes winners) and to inform creative decisions. Practical step: filter by country and category to compare like-for-like.
